extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, rhetoric, public speaking, and grammar
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria for conversation, public speaking, legal advocacy, political leadership, and grammar-writing as discussed in a literary-criticism essay about contemporary figures. Focus is on what qualities make performances, speeches, and grammatical works effective or defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity and vehemence of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The integrity and vehemence of a speaker's manner — the determined way in which he gives himself up to his subject — arrests attention despite other circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that such wholehearted engagement 'fixes it on that, and that alone, which excites such interest and such eagerness in his own breast!' — i.e., personal conviction and force of manner command attention even if other things are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to frame intricate logical argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Possessing a logical theory and the power to weave close and intricate sophistry which entangles hearers or readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'weaves the tissue of his sophistry so close and intricate, that it is difficult not to be entangled in it' and using problematical premises to draw doubtful but possible conclusions — a rhetorical hold that challenges intellects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the pride of the understanding / provocation as charm
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting arguments as a challenge to the intellect — appealing to the reader's pride in understanding — has a subtle, compelling charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay says the mind 'cannot refuse a challenge of strength or skill' and will enter the lists to conquer or be vanquished; this intellectual provocation is a tactic for engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold, sustained, and internally consistent train of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A speaker/writer's train of thought should be bold, well-sustained, and consistent with itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to Dr. Chalmers's discourses: though not elegant, the 'train of thought unfolded at such length and with such strenuousness, was bold, well-sustained, and consistent with itself' — these qualities make lengthy argumentation impressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of thought and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity across a speech or work — a progressive increase in force and coherence — distinguishes superior speakers from those who are merely brilliant in patches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Irving 'wants the continuity of thought and manner' and 'shines by patches and in bursts' rather than building cumulative momentum; continuity is presented as essential to greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine enthusiasm vs performed temperance
rubrics_metrics.description: True, overwhelming enthusiasm that carries a speaker is preferable to a composed, performed temperance which suggests artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts being 'hurried away by a deep or lofty enthusiasm' with having 'self-possession and masterly execution' that creates 'temperance' even amid passion; authenticity engages public audiences more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on mental resources over external advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes speakers who succeed by intellectual force from those who rely on personal appearance or external advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay states Mr. Irving is an example of succeeding by 'external advantages', while Dr. Chalmers shows what can be done 'without them' — implying intrinsic intellectual strength is the higher merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence in private conversation (repartee and personal tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: In private circles, qualities like ready repartee, shrewd cross-question, ridicule, banter, caustic remarks, and amusing anecdotes keep attention and secure triumph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the hallmarks of conversational success: personal contest, momentary advantages, and tactics that gratify hearers' curiosity or self-love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience and medium
rubrics_metrics.description: What succeeds in intimate conversation often fails in public assembly; one must adapt style and content to the audience and setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes 'there is no rule...that which constitutes the excellence of conversation is of little use in addressing large assemblies' — speakers must change tactic for mass audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking must show the speaker is moved and share sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: To move large audiences a speaker must show personal movement and make common cause with the hearers; demonstrate sympathy with predominant public feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author writes 'The way to move great masses of men is to show that you yourself are moved' and that audiences are touched by what affects themselves or the general weal — luminous exposition and zeal are praised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to public causes, not personal vanity
rubrics_metrics.description: In public addresses, the triumph comes from advancing a public cause and expressing sympathy, not from personal display or vanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautions that 'He who thinks first of himself... will be sure to turn attention away from his claims' — make common cause with hearers rather than self.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech structure: continuous momentum (stream) vs isolated epigrams (drops)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful speech should create continuous momentum — a stream — rather than a succession of effective but disconnected sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique: 'His eloquence was a succession of drops, not a stream' — each sentence may be good but the whole must cohere into a speech that advances the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactical suitability: courtroom strengths versus parliamentary limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forums reward different tactics: defensive legal technicality and impenetrability suit courts, while parliament requires momentum and engagement with public questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Tooke 'made the best figure' in court where he could 'stand merely on the defensive' and use 'cross purposes, moot-points, pleas, demurrers, flaws' to baffle opponents; these same tactics failed to move the House of Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leadership requires principle and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A political leader must be bold and represent a cause or party genuinely; mere contrarian cleverness or 'trimming' undermines leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticises Tooke as a 'trimmer' who 'represented nobody but himself' and who 'enticed others into scrapes' — leadership should be principled, not driven by spleen or intellectual exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar/scientific writing: reduce the difficult to principles and the complex to the simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Good grammatical or scientific exposition proceeds by analysis to first principles, explaining the obscure by the plain and the complex by the simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised: Tooke 'clears away the rubbish of school-boy technicalities, and strikes at the root of his subject' and 'did not explain the obscure by the more obscure, but the difficult by the plain' — this is declared 'true principles of science.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar writing must define core terms and avoid unfinished central problems
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should define the fundamental concepts (e.g., the verb) rather than postponing or leaving central definitions unfinished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: after 16 dismissals he 'refers the reader for the true solution to a third volume, which he did not live to finish' — omitting key definitions weakens the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prolix, dogmatical digressions and irrelevant matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous grammatical or philosophical work should avoid prolix dissertations on irrelevant topics; such digressions dilute value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tooke is faulted for 'spun out his great work with prolix and dogmatical dissertations on irrelevant matters' — undermining clarity and focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between methodological claims and practice (avoid metaphysical hypocrisy)
rubrics_metrics.description: If one rejects metaphysical explanations, one should not found a new metaphysical theory; methodological consistency is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay observes that after denying old metaphysical theories of language, Tooke 'should attempt to found a metaphysical theory of his own on the nature and mechanism of language' — a self-contradiction criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not transpose Latin grammatical categories mechanically onto English
rubrics_metrics.description: An English grammar should not be a mere translation of Latin grammatical categories; definitions must fit the language's realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lindley Murray is accused of translating Latin grammar into English and thus defining nouns/verbs/adjectives inappropriately — 'this is an extraordinary stretch of blindness and obstinacy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit from logical acuteness rather than fanciful play
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit that springs from sharp logical combinations and legalistic exactness differs from fancy-driven wit; it may delight but not always yield 'sound and true' observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay suggests Mr. Tooke's wit was 'an excess of his logical faculty' — it 'did not consist in the play of fancy, but in close and cutting combinations of the understanding' and often aimed at exposing flaws in argument rather than imaginative insight.
